question: In written question E-001061/20231, submitted on 29 March 2023, a little known fact is raised: in order to stimulate the growth of in vitro meat cells, manufacturers use foetal bovine serum, for which pregnant cows need to be slaughted. As long as this serum is used, in vitro meat will still contribute to animal abuse.

This is no way to treat our farmers, who are already suffering from unfair competition from non-EU countries and seeing their income decline year on year. To protect their farmers and the country’s world-renowned gastronomy, on 16 November 2023, the Italian Parliament banned the production and marketing of lab-grown meat in Italy. 1.
Will the Commission follow Italy's example by facilitating the adoption of this ban in other Member States?
Can it say whether it funds, directly or indirectly, research projects on in vitro meat?
Now that it is aware of the animal suffering caused by this industry and the structural and lasting nature of the livestock crisis, does the Commission intend to stop any such funding?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.4.2024) The marketing of cell-based meat is subject to the legislation on novel foods and could be placed on the EU market only after an authorisation has been granted by the Commission on the basis of applications submitted by economic operators and following a thorough premarket safety assessment by the European Food Safety Authority.

Until now, the Commission has not received any application for the authorisation of such products. Regarding research activities to improve knowledge on potential environmental, health and social impacts of in vitro meat products, under Horizon 2020, about EUR 4.5 million were provided to four projects focusing on cultured meat (e.g., Meat4All1).

Under Horizon Europe, two calls (EUR 18 million in total) focused or included elements on cultured meat. For example, in the 2023-2024 work programme of Cluster 6 ‘Food, Bioeconomy, Natural Resources, Agriculture and Environment’, a EUR 7 million topic entitled ‘Cultured meat and cultured seafood – state of play and future prospects in the EU’2 was launched, and a project (FEASTS3) has been funded.

As clearly stated in the topic, the objective is to develop a knowledge and evidence base on the potential sustainability aspects of these food products and explore their opportunities and drawbacks. The Commission cannot confirm whether foetal bovine serum (FBS) is used as a culture growth supplement, as this may be product-dependant. In any case, if used, the FBS must be collected in approved slaughterhouses.
All animals in the EU are slaughtered in accordance with Regulation (EC) No. 1099/20094 to minimise suffering of animals during slaughtering.
